prompt:
Return only the prescribed JSON experiment specification.
The question and competing predictions have already been registered. Preserve them.
For contrast: give literal prefix and suffix frames and ONLY the replacement fragments
in conditions; Python concatenates them. No {slot}, markers, full-sentence extraction,
regex, code, or token indices. Conditions apply to every frame. Use multiple frames
when a claim should generalize across contexts, and change only the disputed factor.
The first condition is the reference; each condition declares predictions under both
explanations. Choose replacement_span, after_replacement, or last_token. Scoring is
signed absmax on the declared span, or single on the last token; it excludes common
prefix tokens. after_replacement requires a nonempty suffix; replacement_span requires
nonempty replacements. Respect the supplied token budget; inputs are never truncated.
For corpus: specify two to four labeled groups of literal terms (OR within each group).
The program scans the full archive, excludes initial interpretation documents, samples
matching documents uniformly by fixed seed without seeing activations, and scores the
first matched span. Use genuinely distinguishing groups; no regex or activation filter.

examples.attack: N2 was proposed as narrow suppression of dense unanchored identifiers, not a general non-Colorado suppressor.
examples.prediction: Dense identifiers outside Colorado should be negative, while non-Colorado administrative or natural prose should not be broadly negative.
examples.result: N2 has 58 negative and 2 positive measured cases; nevertheless Foot & Ankle Clinics of Utah phone text and an author-initial block are positive or near zero, and many no-visible non-Colorado cases are positive. This narrows N2 but rejects a broad non-Colorado suppressor.

examples.attack: P4/P5 predicted Colorado local frames should dominate local contacts and unstated Colorado entities.
examples.prediction: If true, Poudre/CU Health/Longmont contacts should be positive, and scheduling-only or other-state contacts should be weak or negative.
examples.result: Controlled tests support positives for Poudre, CU Health, Longmont, Broomfield, and CSU URL, but neutral scheduling desk is near zero and Boise control is weakly positive; P4/P5 survive with specificity, while search strength alone does not prove them.

examples.attack: H4/N3 predicted other-state Natural Heritage labels, not nature or parks, are negative.
examples.prediction: Alaska Natural Heritage should be negative while Colorado Natural Heritage and Colorado/Rocky/Trail nature contexts should be positive or neutral.
examples.result: Alaska label is negative, but Colorado Natural Heritage and Rocky Mountain NP/Trail Ridge are strongly positive; Utah/Montana/Nevada labels remain negative while nearby rare/and tokens are positive. This narrows N3 to program-label branding and rejects broad nature suppression.

claim.title: Colorado/Denver local-entity neuron with narrow unanchored-identifier suppression
claim.lede: The positive pole is driven by explicit Colorado, Denver, or Boulder entities and the local contexts they license—addresses, phone numbers, citations, datelines, state-history enumerations, and nearby spaces, punctuation, or numbers. It also fires for unambiguously Colorado local institutions and landmarks even without the word Colorado. The negative pole is sparse: mostly unanchored dense identifier blocks and one other-state “Natural Heritage” label; broad non-Colorado geography is not supported. Many no-visible-cue cases remain unresolved.
claim.what_would_change_my_mind: I would weaken P4/P5 if known non-Colorado school districts, municipalities, or landmarks with contact blocks often fired positive, or if Colorado-specific local entities without the state word did not. I would revise N2 if dense unanchored identifiers were frequently positive outside a recognized Colorado frame, or if recognized Colorado local institutional frames still produced negative identifier blocks. I would drop N3 if other-state “Natural Heritage” labels were consistently positive. I would broaden the negative pole only if other-state administrative, legal, geographic, or natural contexts reliably and strongly predicted negative responses without Colorado cues; the measured positives among non-Colorado contexts count against that. Unexplained strong responses such as “in Bolivia” or other local-place passages remain unresolved unless a recurring contextual pattern appears.
claim.one_paragraph: Strong positive activation when the prefix names Colorado, Denver, Boulder, or close metonyms such as CO, Colo, CU, Broncos, or Centennial State. The marked token is often a nearby space, punctuation mark, “at”, “is”, or following numeral, but the preceding context contains the place/entity. Exact place tokens are strongest; weaker toponyms need an explicit Colorado frame. Generic place strings, non-Colorado states, and purely geological “Colorado Plateaus” uses without a state/entity frame do not reliably fire. Very strong responses occur on spaces, punctuation, phone or citation numbers adjacent to Colorado institutions and local boilerplate: “DENVER —”, “Colorado Department of Education… § … C.R.S.”, “University of Colorado… 720…”, “Colorado State University Extension… colostate.edu”, “9NEWS”, “Colorado Women’s Education Foundation”. The Colorado entity must be present in the prefix; a bare phone, address, or statute string is not sufficient. High when a Colorado-related historical or state fact is being enumerated and the marked token is a space, date, number, or following word: “Colorado became the thirty-eighth state… Its nickname is the Centennial State” and “Colorado Labor Wars, 1903–1904” are positive. The pattern needs the Colorado frame; bare dates, numbers, or historical lists in other states are weak or negative. Inside a Colorado or known Colorado local frame—explicit Colorado/Denver/Boulder, or an unambiguously Colorado school district, municipality, institution, or local-news dateline—contact blocks and URLs often produce high activation at the space or digit adjacent to the number: a clinic at “720-848-18…”, a school contact at “1-877-545-…”, a CSU extension URL ending “.html”, and the local-media marker “9NEWS”. The local Colorado frame must be in the prefix; a bare 720/303 number or generic contact block is not enough. Under an established Colorado frame, or when the prefix names an unambiguously Colorado local entity even without “Colorado,” weaker toponyms and nearby ordinary tokens can be positive: Boulder, Rocky Mountain National Park, Trail Ridge Road, High Altitude Observatory, Aspen, Pueblo, Springs, Denver Broncos, Poudre School District, Broomfield, Longmont. The same word in another state, generic geology, or a broad western topic does not fire; use only with local Colorado support or an unambiguous Colorado entity.
claim.negative_pole: Strong negative at the central punctuation/digit of dense identifier strings—telephone groups with parentheses or hyphens, ZIP/address fragments, statute/legal citations of the “§ 28-33-02” type, grant IDs, and long comma-grouped area or statistical figures—when the prefix lacks any Colorado/Denver/Boulder frame or an unambiguously Colorado local entity such as Poudre School District, Broomfield, High Altitude Observatory, or Trail Ridge Road. The sign attaches to the whole formatted block, often at a space, comma, hyphen, parenthesis, or single digit. Ordinary dates, small counts, email-only contact labels, geographically nonspecific numbers, and any contact/citation inside a recognized Colorado local institutional frame are weak, unreliable, or positive under P2/P4. Negative for the capitalized label or adjacent token in an other-state natural-heritage program name such as “Alaska Natural Heritage Program” when it is outside a Colorado frame. This does not generalize to nature, wildlife, parks, outdoor recreation, rivers, mountains, or other-state geography: many such non-Colorado natural and geographical passages are positive or neutral. The cue is the program-label construction, not the topic of natural heritage.

examples.rival: The neuron could instead be a general numeric/address/citation detector whose sign depends on whether the string is Colorado-related; if arbitrary Colorado words without nearby numbers fail to fire, this rival gains support.

examples.rival: A competing account is a generic non-Colorado administrative/geographic suppressor; the many positive non-Colorado administrative and natural contexts count against that broad account.

examples.description: The neuron encodes document-level local-entity context: once a Colorado institution, municipality, or dateline appears, many nearby ordinary tokens such as spaces, punctuation, and numbers inherit high activation.
examples.rival: Only the actual place tokens may be encoded, with nearby-token high values being tokenization or output-weighting artifacts; mixed-sign examples such as “Colorado Plateaus” keep this rival alive.

question.question: In natural saved examples, do named non-Colorado school districts, counties, or municipalities with phone/address contact blocks behave like Colorado local contacts (positive), or remain weak/negative?
question.hypothesis: P4/P5 local-contact positivity is Colorado-specific: non-Colorado named local entities with contact blocks remain weak or negative.
question.rival: The neuron responds to generic local civic contact blocks, so some non-Colorado school-district/county/municipal contacts should be positive comparable to Colorado controls.
question.prediction_if_hypothesis: Natural non-Colorado local contact examples should be weak/negative, while Colorado positive controls such as Poudre School District contact blocks remain strongly positive.
question.prediction_if_rival: At least some naturally occurring non-Colorado named school-district/county/municipal contact blocks should show positive activation not explainable by an adjacent Colorado cue.
question.distinguishing_observation: Positive activation for a non-Colorado named school-district/county/municipal contact block comparable to Colorado local-contact controls.
question.why_new: C2 tested controlled Colorado local contacts and a Boise place control, but not natural non-Colorado school-district/municipal contact blocks, which the frozen interpretation explicitly names as a potential weakening condition.

examples.text:
Thu 4 Sep 2014
Filed under: Education,Ethnic Issues,News
Forget your typical school district. If you’re a student in Karen State, what matters most for your education is whether you live in a white, gray or black zone.
Colors on a map. During six decades of civil war, ethnic Karen rebels divided their homeland in this way. White zones were enemy territory, where you would find government soldiers in pressed green uniforms. Farther into the lush jungles, gray zones were contested areas of mixed control, while black zones were held by the rebels themselves.
Education was also split along these lines. In white zones, teachers at government schools spoke Burmese language and taught the government’s approved curriculum. In black zones, the rebel Karen National Union (KNU) ran its own expansive school system, with teachers instructing in Karen language while emphasizing Karen history. In gray zones, especially in the later years of the war, so-called “mixed schools” promoted elements of both curricula.
But now, the distinctions are blurring. Both sides signed a ceasefire deal in 2012, and since then the government and government-approved NGOs have built more schools in mixed and rebel territories. Today, leaders of the KNU’s education department—known as the Karen Education Department (KED)—complain that sometimes the government sends its own teachers to KNU-funded schools and appoints them as headmasters.
Along with political and economic reforms, leaders in Naypyidaw are attempting to overhaul the national education system. In the process, ethnic educators say they fear a “quiet infiltration” into their territory—with government schools arriving first, followed by the necessary administration, such as government-approved village heads and police officers.

COMMITTED TO VISIBLE LEARNING
The question, “What did you learn today?” is vital to our district-wide commitment to Visible Learning. Parents can turn the question, “What did you do today?” into “What did you LEARN” today?” to see Visible Learning in action. It’s not just what students are learning, it’s also about how they are learning. As Visible Learning research has shown, the greatest impact on student learning is collective efficacy. Simply stated, our impact is much greater as we do “MORE TOGETHER.”
What is Visible Learning?
ABOUT OUR DISTRICT
PCSD 25 provides the highest quality educational services in a safe, supportive and caring learning environment for approximately 12,500 students within thirteen elementary schools, four middle schools, three high schools, and an alternative school. Incorporated in 1887, PCSD 25 is located in southeastern Idaho in Bannock County (population: 83,691).

In the spring of 1918, the South Park District’s Board of Commissioners invited Joseph Donnersberger to have a portrait made of himself, which would be displayed in the new McKinley Park field house. Donnersberger, who had previously served on the board for many years, replied that he would take “great pleasure” in receiving this honor. He contacted renowned Chicago artist Lorado Taft, who asked Paul Fjelde, then a sculptor in his studio, to create a bronze bas-relief portrait of Donnersberger. Fjelde’s distinguished bronze panel portrays Donnersberger in profile, with an inscription about his commitment to public service below.
Born in Cincinnati, Ohio, Joseph Donnersberger (1843–1929) moved to Chicago after serving in the Civil War. He established a real estate firm and went on to become president of the Chicago Real Estate Board. Donnersberger was South Park Commissioner from 1889 to 1902 and again from 1911 to 1916. He served as president of the board for ten of those eighteen years, including 1893, the year in which the World’s Columbian Exposition took place in Jackson Park.
Paul Fjelde (1892–1984) was the son of Norwegian immigrant and acclaimed sculptor Jacob Fjelde, who died when Paul was a young child. Despite this untimely death, Fjelde’s mother encouraged her son to become a sculptor. Fjelde studied art at the North Dakota State Normal School.
